hazards.no-scba-entry: You went into the chlorine room with no SCBA staged and nobody outside. A leak in there is one breath from a hospital; the air pack at the door and the operator watching through the window are what turn a leak into a procedure instead of a rescue.
hazards.reused-gasket: You reused the old lead gasket. A lead gasket crushes once to seal; the second time it seals until the pressure comes on and then weeps chlorine at the yoke all night.
hazards.roll-uncapped: You moved a cylinder with the valve uncapped and unhooded. A snapped valve on a 150-lb cylinder empties it into the room in minutes; the cap and hood go on before the cylinder moves an inch.
hazards.water-on-leak: You put water on a chlorine leak. Chlorine and water make hydrochloric acid — the leak corrodes wider, the cloud grows, and the room becomes an entry for a hazmat team.

interrupts.alert: The room monitor has gone into alarm. There is chlorine in the air while you have the cylinder off.
interrupts.cue: Read it. Do not assume it is the sensor.
interrupts.missNote: You carried on changing a cylinder in a room that was alarming. Chlorine at a few parts per million takes your airway before it takes your judgement, and the people who die in these rooms are the ones who assumed the sensor was faulty.
interrupts.why: A chlorine alarm during a changeout is real until proven otherwise, and what it tells you is whether you are leaving or finishing. The reading decides that, not how inconvenient it is.
interrupts.wrongNote: The monitor is what is alarming. Nothing you do at the manifold means anything until you know what the room is reading.

interrupts.alert: The operator outside has opened the door to ask how long you will be. They have no SCBA on.
interrupts.cue: That door stays shut while a leak test is running.
interrupts.missNote: You let an unprotected person stand in the doorway of a room you were pressure-testing chlorine in. If the joint had failed they would have taken the release at face height, and there would have been nobody outside to call it.
interrupts.why: The attendant outside is the person who calls it in and keeps everyone else out. Standing in an open doorway during a leak test makes them the second casualty and leaves nobody to raise the alarm.
interrupts.wrongNote: It is the person in the doorway. Get them out and the door shut before you touch anything else.

lateNotes.ammonia-bottle: The leak test comes after the yoke is snugged — there is nothing to test before the joint is made.
lateNotes.feed-rotameter: Feed rate is set once the cylinder is on line and tested; the rotameter reads nothing until then.
lateNotes.full-valve: The new cylinder opens only after the yoke is tight and the ammonia test is clean — a leak found with the valve open is a release, not a test.

name: Chlorine Room

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the change-out procedure, the feed setpoint and who is the outside operator.
steps.prompt: Check the change-out procedure, the feed setpoint and who is the outside operator.
steps.title: Read the SOP and today's feed rate
steps.why: The SOP names the setpoint the plant needs and the two-person rule for the room, and it exists because a chlorine cylinder change is not a job to improvise under time pressure — every line in it removes one way to end up standing in a room with a rising concentration and no plan already agreed to. The change is done the same way every time so the one time it leaks, the response is a habit already rehearsed, not a decision made from scratch with an alarm already sounding.

steps.cue: Read the chlorine monitor and bump-test it — commit when it reads inside the clean-air band.

gauge.label: ROOM Cl₂
gauge.missNote: Above the clean-air band — do not enter; ventilate and re-read.

steps.prompt: Read the chlorine monitor and bump-test it — commit when it reads inside the clean-air band.
steps.title: Check the room monitor
steps.why: The monitor is the only thing that smells chlorine before you do at a concentration that matters — the OSHA PEL sits well below the level a human nose reliably notices, so by the time you can smell it yourself the room may already be past the ceiling limit. It is read and bump-tested before the door opens every time, because a sensor that has drifted or died is worse than no sensor at all: it tells you the room is clear when it no longer has any way of knowing.

steps.cue: SCBA checked and staged at the door; a second operator outside the room with a radio and eyes on the window.
steps.prompt: SCBA checked and staged at the door; a second operator outside the room with a radio and eyes on the window.
steps.title: Stage the SCBA and post the outside operator
steps.why: Nobody works a chlorine cylinder alone in this room. The pack is staged at the door because the leak, if it comes, comes at the yoke where you are standing — Chlorine Institute Pamphlet 65's Emergency Kit A assumes a response starts within seconds of a release, not minutes, and an SCBA fetched from a locker down the hall after the alarm sounds is a rescue that has already lost the only window that mattered.

steps.cue: Turn the valve on the empty cylinder fully closed with the cylinder wrench.
steps.prompt: Turn the valve on the empty cylinder fully closed with the cylinder wrench.
steps.title: Close the empty cylinder's valve
steps.why: The regulator comes off a closed valve, never an open one — cracking a fitting on a cylinder still under pressure sprays chlorine gas straight at whoever's hands are on the wrench. The cylinder reads 'empty' at roughly 20 lb residual, not zero, and that residual is still under enough vapour pressure to empty itself through any fitting left open, which is exactly why the valve is proven fully closed before anything downstream of it is touched.

steps.cue: Vacuum regulator off the valve, outlet cap on, protective hood over the valve — in that order.
steps.outOfOrderNote: Regulator off, then cap, then hood — the valve is sealed before it is covered.
steps.prompt: Vacuum regulator off the valve, outlet cap on, protective hood over the valve — in that order.
steps.title: Remove the regulator, cap and hood the empty
steps.why: The cap seals the outlet and the hood protects the valve stem for the trip across the room and the ride back to the supplier — Chlorine Institute Pamphlet 1 treats an uncapped valve as the single failure that turns a dropped or rolled cylinder into a full release, because a snapped valve stem on a cylinder this size empties the entire remaining charge in well under a minute with nothing left to shut it off.

steps.cue: Roll the full cylinder from the storage rack, hooded, and seat it on the scale.

drag.missNote: Not on the scale — seat the cylinder on the platform, valve toward the yoke.

steps.prompt: Roll the full cylinder from the storage rack, hooded, and seat it on the scale.
steps.title: Bring the full cylinder onto the scale
steps.why: The scale is how the plant knows what is actually left in service rather than trusting a gauge or a guess: feed is confirmed by weight loss over the shift, and a cylinder is called empty at roughly 20 lb residual rather than run to zero, because a cylinder emptied of usable chlorine still holds a vapour pressure that will happily push whatever residual remains straight out through any fitting left open.

steps.cue: Chain the cylinder upright to the wall bracket, and take a new lead gasket from the sealed pack for the yoke.
steps.prompt: Chain the cylinder upright to the wall bracket, and take a new lead gasket from the sealed pack for the yoke.
steps.title: Chain the cylinder and fit a new gasket
steps.why: A chained cylinder cannot fall on its own valve, and a 150-lb cylinder falling on an unprotected valve stem is exactly the impact that snaps one off. A new lead gasket at every connection is the Chlorine Institute's own rule rather than a convenience, because a lead gasket seals by taking a single controlled crush — reusing one that has already taken that crush leaves a joint that looks tight and weeps chlorine the moment pressure comes up behind it.

steps.cue: Snug the yoke by hand, then a quarter turn with the wrench — commit inside the band.

gauge.label: TURNS PAST SNUG
gauge.missNote: Under- or over-tightened — back off and bring it to a quarter turn past snug.

steps.prompt: Snug the yoke by hand, then a quarter turn with the wrench — commit inside the band.
steps.title: Tighten the yoke
steps.why: The lead gasket seals by taking a controlled crush, and a quarter turn past hand-tight is the amount of crush that seals the joint without going further: less than that and the gasket never fully seats, so it weeps chlorine at the yoke as soon as pressure comes on; more than that crushes the gasket into the valve threads and leaves a damaged sealing face that the next change inherits whether or not the gasket itself gets replaced.

steps.cue: Hold the ammonia bottle's vapour under the yoke, the regulator and the valve packing — a white cloud is a leak.
steps.holdBreakNote: You lifted the bottle before every joint was covered — start the test again.
steps.prompt: Hold the ammonia bottle's vapour under the yoke, the regulator and the valve packing — a white cloud is a leak.
steps.title: Ammonia leak test every joint
steps.why: Ammonia vapour meets chlorine gas and makes a visible white ammonium chloride cloud at a concentration of only a few parts per million, well below what most people can smell and far below anything an eye could catch on a bare joint — which is why every yoke, every regulator fitting and every valve packing gets tested with the bottle before the cylinder goes into service, not just the ones that look suspect.

steps.cue: Open the new cylinder's valve one full turn — no more — and leave the wrench on the stem.
steps.prompt: Open the new cylinder's valve one full turn — no more — and leave the wrench on the stem.
steps.title: Open the valve one turn
steps.why: One full turn of a chlorine cylinder valve gives full flow through the regulator; turning it further only adds turns that have to be found again by feel if the valve needs shutting fast in a leak. The wrench stays seated on the stem for exactly that reason — the first motion in an emergency has to be closing the valve, and a wrench that has to be located first is seconds a chlorine release in an enclosed room does not give back.

steps.cue: Adjust the rotameter to the SOP setpoint and commit inside the band.

gauge.label: FEED RATE
gauge.missNote: Off the setpoint — re-adjust the rotameter to the SOP feed rate.

steps.prompt: Adjust the rotameter to the SOP setpoint and commit inside the band.
steps.title: Set the feed rate
steps.why: The setpoint is the chlorine residual the plant is required to hold at the customer's tap, not a number set to look busy on the rotameter: too little and pathogens the disinfection step exists to kill can survive the required contact time, too much and the plant fields taste-and-odour complaints while paying to feed chlorine that leaves through the vent as unused excess residual.

steps.cue: Check the in-service cylinder, the kit and the door, and click what is not as it should be.

itemNotes.wrench-missing: The cylinder wrench is on the bench, not on the in-service valve stem — in a leak, the first thing you need would not be there.

steps.prompt: Check the in-service cylinder, the kit and the door, and click what is not as it should be.
steps.title: Walk the room before leaving
steps.why: The room is left the way the next leak — not this shift's leak, whichever one comes next — actually needs it: the wrench seated on the in-service valve stem where an emergency response starts, Kit A sealed and within reach rather than checked once a quarter, the door closed, and the monitor confirmed live rather than assumed live because it was live yesterday.

tagline: 150-lb chlorine cylinder change: room monitor and SCBA before the door, empty isolated and capped, full one on the scale and chained, new gasket, yoke a quarter turn past snug, ammonia leak test, valve one turn, wrench on the stem
